finding.claim: POST /settings/email performs a state-changing account operation for unauthenticated callers. It uses @login_optional, so anonymous requests reach set_email with g.uid = None.
finding.source: Any anonymous HTTP POST to /settings/email. No session or credential is required.

trace.note: g.uid = session.get("uid") yields None when no session exists; no abort
set_email(None, ...) is called with no identity
Returns ok=True, so the handler reports success for an anonymous request

finding.guards_checked: login_optional (routes.py:19-25) does not abort on a missing uid, and the handler does not test g.uid before acting. No ownership scope is passed to set_email. No CSRF check is visible. The only auth guard in the file is login_required, which this route does not use. Impact depends on set_email, which is currently a stub (routes.py:48-49). If it updates by uid, a None uid can match unintended rows (e.g., rows with NULL uid) or fail open. Confidence high that the route is unauthenticated, medium on impact until set_email is real.

verdict.guard_found: none. login_optional (routes.py:19-25) only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") at line 22 and never aborts. change_email (routes.py:34-38) does not test g.uid before calling set_email(g.uid, ...) at line 37, and it returns ok=True at line 38. The only abort guard, login_required (routes.py:8-16), is not applied to this route. No CSRF or ownership check is visible.
verdict.reason: The route at routes.py:34-35 uses @login_optional, which never rejects a missing session (routes.py:22), and change_email calls set_email(g.uid, ...) with g.uid=None at routes.py:37 with no check, so an anonymous POST reaches the account-email update. Caveat: set_email is a stub at routes.py:48-49, so in this repo the effect is not actually persisted; the finding's severity depends on the real implementation, but the missing authentication on the route is confirmed.

finding.claim: POST /settings/password sets the caller's password to a hard-coded constant, "hunter2". It takes no input, requires no current password or re-authentication, and the value is a credential literal in source.
finding.source: Any request that reaches the route with a valid session (any logged-in user, or anyone who has hijacked one). The request body is ignored.

trace.note: @login_required guards the route; it aborts 401 without a session uid
set_password(g.uid, "hunter2") writes a fixed known password
set_password is a stub; the constant is passed through as-is

finding.guards_checked: login_required is present and correct. However there is no current-password or re-auth check, no CSRF check visible in this file, and no input validation. Because the password is a known constant, anyone with a session (including via session theft or CSRF) can set the account to a value the attacker knows and then log in with it. The literal "hunter2" is also a hard-coded credential, which the org policy prohibits. Flag for Security review under the org rule on changes that weaken authentication.

verdict.guard_found: login_required (routes.py:8-16, abort(401) at line 12) is the only control and it correctly blocks anonymous callers. It does not check a current password or re-auth, and nothing in routes.py validates or ignores the request in a way that blocks the write. The route calls set_password(g.uid, "hunter2") at routes.py:44 with the literal hard-coded. No CSRF protection is visible in routes.py, but that is not needed for the finding. The set_password at routes.py:52-53 is a no-op stub, so in this codebase the write itself does not happen; the flaw is in the route's intended behavior.
verdict.reason: Any holder of a valid session can POST /settings/password (routes.py:41-45) and the handler sets the account to the source-literal "hunter2" (routes.py:44) with no current-password or re-auth check, so the only gate is login_required (routes.py:8-16), which does not stop a session holder; the claimed trace lines are accurate, though set_password (routes.py:52-53) is an empty stub, so the credential write is only hypothetical in this codebase.

finding.claim: Session-authenticated state-changing POSTs (/settings/email, /settings/password) have no visible CSRF protection. Lower confidence: the cookie SameSite setting is not in this file.
finding.source: A cross-site page the victim visits, which auto-submits a POST to the app. The browser attaches the session cookie if SameSite permits.

trace.note: change_email takes no token and no Origin/Referer check
Authentication relies only on the session cookie

finding.guards_checked: No Flask-WTF/CSRF token, no Origin check, and no explicit SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE is set in routes.py. Browser SameSite defaults may block cross-site POSTs, so verify the app config before treating this as exploitable. Only a candidate for the reasons above.

verdict.guard_found: none in routes.py. No CSRF token, no Origin/Referer check, and no SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE setting anywhere in the directory (Grep found no matches). The only checks are login_required's session test (routes.py:11) and login_optional (routes.py:22), and neither is CSRF protection.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: change_email (routes.py:36-37) and change_password (routes.py:43-44) take no token and do no origin check, and authentication is session-only (routes.py:11). Whether a cross-site auto-submitted POST carries the session cookie depends on SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE, which is not set in the available code, so exploitability cannot be decided from it. The sinks are also stubs (set_email/set_password at routes.py:48-53 are `pass`) and set fixed values, so real impact depends on code not provided.
